title: Russia and US discussing sanctions relief for Moscow’s sovereign wealth fund, Kremlin aide says | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The Trump administration and the Kremlin are discussing the possible lifting of US sanctions on Russia’s multibillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund, Russian state media quoted a Kremlin aide as saying, in what would be another US concession to Moscow in negotiations to end itswar in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that talks with the United States to lift sanctions on the state-owned Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) have been “going on for some time,” Russian state news agency TASS reported on Wednesday.

“What the outcome will be, I do not know,” he added.

The fund’s CEO and presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev was actively engaging American officials on lifting the sanctions, Ushakov said.

A US official said Dmitriev “has been a helpful envoy to US negotiators in discussions” to end the war in Ukraine.

“The administration is undergoing its normal process in assessing RDIF’s de-listing application in an effort to improve U.S.-Russia relations and help end the war,” the official said.

The Biden administration imposed the sanctions in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, calling it a “known slush fund” for Putin and his inner circle.

The New York Times first reported on Tuesday that the Trump administration was considering lifting the sanctions.

President Donald Trump hasdefended recent concessionsmade to Russia on sanctions, which have triggered criticism from both sides of the aisle in Washington anddriven a wedgebetween the US and its Western allies.

Earlier this month, Trump announced a deal to allowRussian diesel exportsto global energy markets and waived a furtherslate of sanctionsrelated to Russian fossil fuel sales that had only just been signed into law.

The forestalled legislation would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on, among other things, goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, the sale of which is crucial to funding the Kremlin’s war machine.

The US-Russia diesel deal involvessuspending fuel export sanctionsfor six months to allow for diesel sales at market prices, but experts have cast doubt on the impact it will have on global diesel markets.

Russiabanned exports of dieselin early July, after Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries triggered widespread fuel shortages across the country.

The White House is trying to relieve pressure on oil and diesel prices in the US ahead of crucial midterm elections next week.

Trump has also said his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia was to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on October 18.

Trump has blamed high global fuel prices on Ukraine, and heaped pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymr Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian refineries even as Russia continues its attacks on Ukraine’s towns, cities, and energy infrastructure.

There is growing anxiety in Kyiv and Europe that the Trump administration will make further concessions to Moscow in an effort to get Putin to agree to a peace deal.

Zelensky recently told NBC’s “Meet the Press” that the waivers strengthened Putin’s war against Ukraine while Moscow was failing on the battlefield.

Kyiv has long advocated for tougher sanctions on Russian energy exports.

Last week, Putin said the Kremlin would beready to resumetrilateral Russia-US-Ukraine peace talks after mid-November, at the request of US special envoy Steve Witkoff who met the Russian leader in St. Petersburg. During the talks, Putin expressed interest in restoring economic cooperation with the US.

CNN’s Anna Chernova, Kevin Liptak, David Goldman, Matt Egan, Ivana Kottasová, Jennifer Hansler, Tim Lister and Daria Tarasova-Markina contributed to this report.
